pr_title: Add a well-known Secrets key for CA certificate bundles.
pr_body:
**What type of PR is this?**

/kind feature

**What this PR does / why we need it**:

Add a well-known key for storing the CA certificate bundle in TLS
secrets. This key is supported by cert-manager and a number of Ingress
controller projects.

Add support for creating secrets with the new key to kubectl.

**Which issue(s) this PR fixes**:

Fixes #91353.

**Special notes for your reviewer**:

**Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?**:
<!--
If no, just write "NONE" in the release-note block below.
If yes, a release note is required:
Enter your extended release note in the block below. If the PR requires additional action from users switching to the new release, include the string "action required".

For more information on release notes see: https://git.k8s.io/community/contributors/guide/release-notes.md
-->
```release-note
Adds the `--ca` flag to the the `kubectl create secret tls` command.
Adds the `TLSCABundleKey` constant.
```

issue_context.title: Add a well-known Secret key constant for CA certificate bundles
issue_context.body:
**What would you like to be added**:

Add a constant `TLSCABundleKey = "ca.crt" to the set of well known names that are used to key Secret data.

**Why is this needed**:

Most Ingress controllers provide a TLS termination feature and support using TLS Secrets to specify the server certificate and private key. A number of projects in the ecosystem (e.g. certificate-manager, contour, ingress-nginx) also support specifying the CA certificate bundle in the "ca.crt" key. certificate-manager is particularly important here, since it will populate that key automatically in secrets that it generates.

Adding a standard key name constant in Kubernetes will make the use of "ca.crt" officially blessed and improve standardization and interoperability in the Ingress ecosystem.

review_comments: If this is the intermediates, don't we need to check that they form a chain up from the cert itself?

Yeh, in principle we could do this, but I'm wary of second-guessing exactly how organizations build certificate hierarchies. I was afraid of the risk of having to tweak this logic over multiple releases :)

The typical requirement for a CA bundle is not that it is associated with the certificate being presented, but that it is valid for the certificates presented by the remote end of the TLS connection. The relationship between the CA bundle and the cert/key is unclear to me.

Typically, when a CA issues a server certificate, they don't issue it from the trusted root, but from an intermediate CA that they can invalidate if necessary. Client applications don't have the intermediate CA certificates in their trust stores, but only the public root. 

When a CA issues a certificate to a user, the CA will provide both the leaf server certificate, and a bundle of intermediate certificates to establish the chains of trust to the trusted root. This bundle is the CA bundle that is invariably needed when setting up a TLS server.

So when you use a Secret to store a TLS certificate for Ingress, you also need some way to specify the CA bundle. cert-manager does it using the `ca.crt` key and a number of Ingress controllers support this scheme due to the popularity of cert-manager.

https://letsencrypt.org/certificates/
https://www.sslmarket.com/ssl/intermediate-and-root-certificates-ca-bundle/

In the Let's Encrypt case, on macOS I only have the "ISRG Root X1" certificate in my system keychain, but they actually issue certificates from "Let’s Encrypt Authority X3". This means that any server using a Let's Encrypt certificate must be configured with the CA bundle so that the server can send the intermediate certificates and the client can establish the chain of trust.

Intermediates are often appended to the certificate content itself. The common uses of ca.crt I've seen are to specify a bundle to use to verify the other actor, not as a bundle of intermediates to present. Mixing up the two uses would lead to verification bugs.

Appending to certificate content is what I have seen as well for handling intermediates.

(repeating what was said above)
Isn't ca.crt usually the trusted root?

The reason we support the CA bundle (with any combination of root and intermediate) certificates in Contour is because cert-manager generates them. IIUC, cert-manager generates them because of ingress-nginx supports https://github.com/jetstack/cert-manager/pull/848. It's not immediately obvious to me whether the Istio support in https://github.com/istio/istio/pull/22622  is for client or server certificates.

I haven't seen this field used for specifying the CA to validate a TLS peer against, and from my perspective, it seems a bit unnatural to bundle that with a client certificate, since (at least in principle), it might be different for each peer.

How would you recommend we proceed here?

1. Drop the PR?
2. Drop the just kubectl changes?
3. Update the doc comment for the key constant to be neutral WRT how to use the key?

> I haven't seen this field used for specifying the CA to validate a TLS peer

IIUC, that's exactly what ingress-nginx does, see https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx/examples/auth/client-certs/#creating-certificate-secrets:

> You can create a secret containing CA certificate along with the Server Certificate, that can be used for both TLS and Client Auth.
>
>> kubectl create secret generic ca-secret --from-file=tls.crt=server.crt --from-file=tls.key=server.key --from-file=ca.crt=ca.crt

tls.crt/tls.key are the presented serving certificate

ca.crt is the CA bundle used to verify the TLS peer certificates

> How would you recommend we proceed here?

If we want to identify recommended keys for uses, I think we should be as clear as possible, not neutral or ambiguous about the meaning of a file that can cause significant security problems if used for an unexpected purpose.

For example, if we needed to recommend a separate filename to contain intermediate certs to present, a name like `intermediates.crt` would be much clearer (though I still am more familiar with the approach of appending intermediates to the certificate file).

Hmm, in that case I'm probably not the right person to take this forward. The use of ca.crt as a peer validation root isn't a pattern that I'm familiar with or really feel comfortable advocating here.

Thanks for reviewing and taking the time to discuss this :)

this isn't typically what a ca.crt means... I have similar questions to what I raised in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/91222#issuecomment-630531596

When an actor is consuming a cert/key pair in order to make a TLS connection, the cert/key is typically what they present to the other party, and the ca.crt bundle is what they use to verify the certificate presented by the other party. There is no inherent relationship between the CAs that issued the two certificates (and in fact it is common for different CAs to issue client and serving certs). I'm not sure bundling the CA used to verify the remote connection with the cert/key presented to assert identity makes sense.

I was approaching this from the server certificate perspective, so the CA bundle would be the intermediate certificates leading from the certificate in the secret to the trusted root. If you are doing TLS client auth, I think that this makes sense too, since the server may need the client's intermediate certificates to validate its chain.

This field isn't intended to be the CA that you validate a TLS peer against. Maybe the description needs some additional language to make that clearer.

> This field isn't intended to be the CA that you validate a TLS peer against

It's already being used that way by some clients. See https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx/examples/auth/client-certs/

I'm not that familiar with the code but it looks like ingress-nginx supports the key [generically](https://github.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/blob/master/internal/ingress/controller/store/backend_ssl.go#L37).

Maybe I should have said "my intention in proposing this key is not that it be the CA that you validate the TLS peer against" :)

If the key is already used for conflicting purposes, maybe updating the language here to be more neutral and just say that it is used for a CA certificates?
